TheSaS4DworkflowisdescribedinRef.[52]. OntheleftofFig.12isasingleimagecollectedbythe SaS4D handheld scanner during a scan of a warehouse facility used by NER personnel. This image (and 100s of others) was automatically labeled using a pre-trained neural network, which was used to assign semantic labels to a 3D model generated from the scan. The ability to assign semantic information to the 3D models that SDF is capable of generating provides a basis for enabling volumetric imaging within particular objects. A related NA-22 project, Container Counting within NA-22 Objective L showed the ability to train a neural network to identify a specific container type andtothenuseahandheldsystem(calledC-LAMP)toautomaticallylocateandlabelthoseobjects while performing a scan. This object recognition could be used to incorporate prior knowledge of container (or other object) designs when performing attenuation corrections in volumetric imaging, it can also be used to identify particular objects of interest for SDF analysis and autonomous navigation logic. For example, if an autonomous free-moving SDF-capable system reconstructs high activity on a semantically identified wall, the system could autonomously infer that the source of the activity is likely to be on the other side of the wall, rather than the wall itself. Semantic labeling, attenuation aware algorithms and autonomy are three areas where active research has advanced the SDF state-of-the-art during the RDF project, yet further R&D will be necessary for these capabilities to readily benefit end-users. 2.3.6 Spectral analyses Typically, the count rates used for SDF solutions (e.g., in Eq. 4) are simply count rates over some energy interval set by the user upon observation of a spectroscopic anomaly during data acquisition, due to a spectroscopic alarm from analyses software running onboard the SDF system, or due to prior information (e.g., searching from 137Cs contamination).
